name: Metrics
intent: Record cheap numbers about a system over time (rates, levels, latencies) so you can see trends and problems at a glance, and learn why averages hide the slow requests that users feel.
scenario: A checkout API has an average response time of 120 ms and the dashboard is green. Meanwhile, one customer in a hundred waits several seconds and is giving up.
problem: Logs describe individual events and become expensive when you only want a count. You also need something compact that shows the health of the whole system now and over weeks. And the most common summary, the average, is misleading for latency: a few very slow requests barely move it, but those are the ones people complain about.

howItWorks.title: Three basic metric types
howItWorks.text: A counter only goes up (requests served, errors) and is turned into a rate over time. A gauge goes up and down (queue length, memory in use, active connections). A histogram counts how many observations fell into each range (latency buckets), which is what lets you compute percentiles.

howItWorks.title: Measure the golden signals
howItWorks.text: For a service, start with latency (how long requests take), traffic (how many), errors (how many fail) and saturation (how full the scarce resource is). For a resource, use utilisation, saturation and errors. A few well-chosen metrics tell you more than hundreds of random ones.

howItWorks.title: Percentiles, not averages, for latency
howItWorks.text: The p50 (median) is the typical request. The p95 and p99 are what the slowest 5% and 1% of requests experience. Because one user action often makes many calls, the chance of hitting a slow one is much higher than 1%. Alert and set targets on p95 or p99.

howItWorks.title: Add labels, but keep them few
howItWorks.text: Labels such as service, endpoint and status code let you slice a metric. Every distinct combination becomes a separate time series that is stored and indexed, so never use unbounded values (user id, request id, full URL) as labels. This is the 'cardinality' problem.

howItWorks.title: Collect, store and graph over time
howItWorks.text: Services expose metrics, a collector scrapes or receives them every few seconds, and a time-series database (Prometheus, a cloud monitoring service) stores them cheaply for months. Dashboards and alerts are built from queries on that data.

pros: Very cheap to store compared with logs, so you can keep months of history
Show trends, capacity and the health of the whole system at a glance
The basis for dashboards, alerts and SLOs
Percentiles expose the tail that users actually feel
cons: Aggregates cannot tell you about one specific request
High-cardinality labels can overwhelm the metrics store
Choosing what to measure takes thought, and bad metrics create false comfort
Percentiles cannot be averaged across servers, so histograms must be combined correctly
whenToUse: Always: request rate, errors, latency and saturation for every service
Capacity planning and trend questions such as 'is it getting slower?'
Anything you want to alert on
whenNotToUse: To investigate one particular user's request (use logs and traces)
Labels with unbounded values such as user ids or request ids
pitfalls: Watching the average latency instead of p95 or p99
Averaging percentiles from different servers, which gives a meaningless number
Unbounded label values that create millions of time series
Dashboards with dozens of graphs nobody reads and no clear 'is it healthy?' view
